geo_headlines: STRIKE OR DEAL: TRUMP KEEPS BOTH OPEN. Trump said Saturday the US is considering a possible attack on Iran as soon as Sunday, or could reach "a major deal" (Al Jazeera). The WSJ reported the USS George Washington is being rearmed with bunker-buster bombs and standoff missiles (via Gulf News). **No US strike had been reported as of Sunday morning; Brent ($116.72) and WTI ($103.27) reopen at 6 PM ET.**

IRAN: MIXED SIGNALS. Iran's ambassador in Islamabad said Tehran would reopen Hormuz if the US lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports; an IRGC-linked source called that "lies and fantasy" (Iran International). Speaker Ghalibaf said the US is in a "quagmire" (Al Jazeera). Iran's army said it shot down a US drone over Bandar Abbas (Reuters).

SHIPPING AND SAUDI ARABIA. October has had 28 confirmed or reported ship attacks around Hormuz, the most of any month of the war (Washington Institute via MarineLink). Saudi Arabia intercepted 10 Houthi ballistic missiles Sunday morning, and Riyadh's main airport reopened two weeks after Houthi strikes closed it (Al Jazeera). The Houthis targeted Saudi pumping stations and the east-west pipeline Saturday (Le Monde).

THE WEEK: AI DOUBTS, THEN OIL. S&P 500 7,623.68 (-0.47% week), 2.50% below its October 6 record close; Nasdaq 100 -0.79% after Thursday's -2.9% on Meta, Lam and Tesla; Dow +0.41%. Brent +6.2% to $116.72, the highest since April. 10-year 5.00%, down 9bp after Thursday's biggest drop since March 2023 (Yahoo Finance). FedWatch as of Friday: October 7.8%, December 77.2%. Bitcoin $80,282.79.

THIS WEEK: FED AND MEGACAPS. Monday: Verizon. Tuesday: Coca-Cola, Boeing, UPS, then Visa. Wednesday: FOMC at 2:00 PM; Alphabet (4:30 PM) and Microsoft (5:30 PM). Thursday: third-quarter GDP and September PCE at 8:30 AM; Amazon, Lilly, Mastercard. Friday: employment cost index (StockTitan, CNBC).
client_frame_short: The weekend raised the stakes on oil. Trump said the US could strike Iran as soon as Sunday or reach a major deal, and US carriers are loading heavy munitions. **No strike had happened by Sunday morning, but the risk to watch when futures reopen Sunday evening is a jump in oil from Friday's $116.72.** This week also brings the Fed on Wednesday and results from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon. For clients: this is exactly why diversified portfolios hold bonds and real assets, and plans do not need to change.
client_frame:
If a client calls today, the story is that the weekend raised the odds of either a strike or a deal, and oil will tell us which first.

What changed: Trump said Saturday the US could attack Iran as soon as Sunday, or reach a major deal. The Wall Street Journal reported a US carrier is being loaded with bunker-buster bombs. Iran sent mixed signals: one envoy offered to reopen Hormuz if the US lifts its blockade, while a Revolutionary Guard source denied it. No strike had been reported by Sunday morning.

Where we stand: last week the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq 100 0.8%, while the Dow rose. Brent rose about 6% to $116.72, the highest since April. Bonds rallied, with the 10-year at 5.00%.

Two paths: a strike would likely push oil higher at first and weigh on stocks; a deal that reopens Hormuz would likely send oil sharply lower and help both stocks and bonds. Markets cannot know which, and neither can we. That is why portfolios are built for both, and why guessing the outcome with client money is a bet, not a plan. High-quality bonds have been rallying on fear and paying about 5% while they do it.

This week: the Fed decides Wednesday, with markets pricing about an 8% chance of a hike. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon report, and GDP and PCE inflation come out Thursday.

Why it matters: geopolitical shocks have historically hit markets hard at first and faded within weeks to months, unless they cause a lasting recession.

For clients: stay invested, rebalance toward targets, and avoid making decisions on a weekend headline. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (Friday 5.00%), a 30-year above 5.75% (Friday 5.33%), or US strikes on Iran that keep Brent well above $105 (Friday $116.72). Brent is there; a strike is the missing piece, and the weekend made it more likely.
